opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what drew me in was this striking contrast: these models can do things that seemed out of reach just a few years ago, yet they can fail in ways that feel almost absurd. A model that writes fluent essays or recognizes thousands of object categories can be thrown off by a tiny, imperceptible change to an input, or by a shift in the data it sees once deployed, like images from a different hospital or text in a slightly different style.

That gap between impressive average-case performance and surprising worst-case brittleness felt like something we really needed to understand. As these systems move into high-stakes settings, it isn't enough that they work well on a benchmark. We need to know when and why they break, and whether we can anticipate it.

It's also intellectually fascinating. A lot of our intuitions from classical machine learning, like the idea that more data or bigger models should make things more robust, don't always hold up. Sometimes scaling helps, sometimes it doesn't, and sometimes it introduces new failure modes. So studying failures is a way to probe what these models are actually learning. Are they picking up the underlying structure of the task, or are they latching onto shortcuts and spurious correlations that happen to work on the training distribution?

For me, failures are a lens into the models. If you understand how something breaks, you usually understand a lot more about how it works, and that's what you need to build systems that are reliable and trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response says highly capable models can be thrown off by a tiny, imperceptible input change, clearly describing adversarial-example brittleness.

r002.rationale: It states that working well on a benchmark is not enough and that we need to know when and why models break.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what drew me in was a kind of puzzle that was hard to look away from. When I started my PhD, deep learning was doing remarkably well on the benchmarks we cared about, and yet these same models were strikingly easy to break. You could add a tiny, imperceptible perturbation to an image and flip the prediction, or shift the data distribution just slightly and watch accuracy fall off a cliff. That tension really bothered me. How can something be so capable and so fragile at the same time?

And the more I looked, the more I felt like the failures were actually more informative than the successes. When a model gets something right, it's hard to tell what it has really learned. When it fails, you get a window into the shortcuts it's taking, the spurious correlations it's leaning on, the gap between what we wanted it to learn and what it actually learned. So failures became, for me, a way to understand what's really going on inside these systems.

The other thing is that I came into this from a more theoretical background, and I was interested in whether we could say anything principled about robustness. Early on there were these surprising results, like adversarial training actually hurting standard accuracy, or more data sometimes making things worse in the adversarial setting. Those are counterintuitive, and they suggested that our usual intuitions from standard machine learning don't carry over cleanly. That felt like a very rich space, where there were both deep conceptual questions and immediate practical stakes, since these models were increasingly being deployed in the real world.

So I'd say it was a combination of intellectual curiosity about why these things break and a sense that if we want to trust these systems, we need to understand their failure modes, not just celebrate their average-case performance.

r001.rationale: The response describes tiny, imperceptible image perturbations that flip predictions, showing that capable models can be broken by seemingly small changes.

r002.rationale: It contrasts strong benchmark performance with failures under small perturbations or distribution shifts, indicating benchmark scores alone do not capture those failures.

astra-6.text:
What drew me in was the gap between how capable these models are and how surprisingly they can fail. You can have a model that performs extremely well on a task, but a small change to its input causes it to make a mistake that seems obvious to a person. That raises a really interesting question: what has the model actually learned, and when can we trust it?

I wanted to understand those failures as a way of understanding the models themselves. If we can identify what makes a system brittle, we can start thinking about how to build systems whose reliability matches their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me in was the gap between how well these models perform and how brittle they can be. You can have a model that does extremely well on a test set, but then a small change to the input causes it to make a mistake that seems obvious to a person. That raises a really interesting question: what has the model actually learned, and how does that differ from what we wanted it to learn?

I was interested in understanding that gap, both as a scientific question and because it matters if we want to rely on these systems. Studying failures gives us a way to probe what’s missing and, hopefully, build models whose behavior we can trust more.

r001.rationale: It describes small input changes causing obvious mistakes, but does not identify these as adversarial examples.

r002.rationale: It contrasts strong test-set performance with failures after small input changes, conveying that test scores alone do not capture model failures.
